system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-09-20 07:39:00 to 2173-10-01 19:31:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with ongoing abdominal pain that worsened after eating, consistent with an acute on chronic flare. She had been on TPN since a recent admission but experienced increased pain after oral intake. Lipase and liver enzymes were normal, and MRCP showed chronic pancreatitis changes with stable pancreatic cysts, no acute inflammation. She remained on TPN and was managed with IV then oral pain medications, including an increase in her fentanyl patch to 100 mcg/hour. Pain improved with minimal oral intake. Iron deficiency anemia was confirmed with a ferritin of 9.8, and outpatient plans were made for colonoscopy and possible IV iron. Constipation, worsened by narcotics, was treated with increased bowel regimen. She was discharged home on TPN with visiting nurse services, follow-up arranged with GI, and instructions for repeat pancreatic imaging in 12 months.

radiology_notes.text:
PATIENT HISTORY:  ___ woman with new onset fevers and reflux, assess
for pneumonia or aspiration.

COMPARISON: Chest x-ray ___.

FINDINGS:  New right lower lobe opacity is compatible with aspiration
pneumonia.  Lung is otherwise clear.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal. Wedge deformities of
the lower thoracic spine.

IMPRESSION:  New right lower lobe opacity is suspicious for aspiration
pneumonia.

HISTORY:  ___ -year-old female requiring TPN 

COMPARISON:  PICC line placement ___.  

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___, present and supervising throughout the
procedure, Dr. ___ fellow)

FLUOROSCOPY:  Total fluoro time 7.17 min, 27 mGy.  10 cc of Optiray 320 used. 


PROCEDURE:

Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the patent and compressible
right brachial vein was accessed using a micropuncture needle ultrasound
guidance, and an 018 wire was inserted, however could not be passed beyond the
subclavian vein.  The inner dilator of the micropuncture system was inserted
into the vein, and a brief venogram demonstrated a tight central subclavian
vein stenosis.  Multiple attempts to cross the stenosis with a long Nitinol
wire and 018 glidewire were unsuccessful.  

The patient was repositioned on the fluoroscopy table and the left arm was
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  Access to the left basilic
vein was obtained under ultrasound guidance and an 018 wire was easily passed
into the superior vena cava.  The estimated measurement for the catheter was
44 cm.   Digital images were stored before and after ultrasound access.  

A peel-away sheath was then placed over the guidewire in the left basilic vein
and a double-lumen PICC line measuring 40 cm in length was then placed through
the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in the SVC under fluoroscopic
guidance.  Position of the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot image
of the chest.  

Peel-away sheath and guidewire were then removed.  The catheter was secured to
the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing was applied.  

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.  

FINDINGS:

Severe right subclavian stenosis preventing passage of an 018 wire from the
right arm access.

IMPRESSION:

Severe right subclavian stenosis precluding right arm PICC access at this
time.

Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopically guided 5 ___ double-lumen
PICC line placement via the left basilic venous approach.  Final internal
length is 44 cm with the tip positioned in the SVC.  The line is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were transferred here due to abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pain started about five days ago. It’s in my upper belly and goes straight through to my back. It feels hot and dull, and it doesn’t stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better when I stay still and don’t talk. Breathing deeply makes it worse. I’ve also been vomiting every two hours—greenish, not bloody.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds very uncomfortable. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis, this seems like a flare-up. We’ll keep you on bowel rest—no food or drink—for now to let your pancreas calm down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had these flares before. I usually end up needing IV fluids and pain meds. Is that what you’ll do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you IV fluids, pain medication, and anti-nausea drugs. We’ve already started your fentanyl patch and IV hydromorphone as needed. We’ll monitor your labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My last flare was months ago, but this one feels worse. I’m worried I won’t be able to eat again without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it step by step. Right now, your lipase was elevated, and your exam shows tenderness in the upper abdomen—consistent with pancreatitis. We’ll repeat labs tomorrow to track your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white blood cell count is a bit low at 4.4, but stable. Hemoglobin is 10.6, which is consistent with your known anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired? I know I’ve been anemic for a while, but it’s worse now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that could be part of it. We’re not planning a transfusion now, but we’ll keep an eye on it. Your liver enzymes and kidney function are normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is a little better today, especially when I’m not moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep you NPO for now. We may try clear liquids tomorrow if you continue improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray this morning because you had a slight fever. There’s a new opacity in your right lower lung—likely aspiration pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration? From vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When you vomit, especially if you’re lying down, stomach contents can get into the lungs. We’ll start antibiotics—levofloxacin and metronidazole—for six days to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my stomach? I’m already so nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give the antibiotics IV, so they won’t irritate your stomach. We’re also continuing your anti-nausea meds—ondansetron and promethazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I just want to get past this pneumonia and the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood and urine cultures came back with no growth, which is great—it means no bloodstream infection. The pneumonia treatment is on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I try sipping water today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try clear liquids later today—water, broth—if your nausea stays under control. But we’ll watch closely. In past flares, eating has worsened your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every time. Even small amounts hurt. Maybe I should just stay on IV fluids longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried clear liquids yesterday, but your pain increased. So we’re stopping oral intake again. We’re concerned you’ll need longer nutritional support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I knew it. Every time I try to eat, it flares up. What are my options?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to start TPN—total parenteral nutrition—through a central IV line. It delivers calories, protein, and nutrients directly into your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like I had last year? It helped, but the line was tricky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll place a PICC line, likely in your left arm, since imaging shows a blockage in the right side. The radiology team will do it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local numbing medicine. Most patients tolerate it well. The line will let us give TPN safely and avoid stressing your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is stable. Still nauseous, but the meds help. I’m anxious about the PICC line tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The team will explain each step. You’ll be awake but comfortable. We’ll monitor your vitals the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the PICC line was placed successfully in your left arm. No complications. The radiology report mentioned a blockage in the right subclavian vein, which is why we used the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. Just pressure. Is the TPN starting now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll begin the TPN infusion this afternoon. It will run for 18 hours a day, starting at 6 PM. You’ll still be NPO except for sips and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t eat at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. Your body needs time to heal. TPN will keep you nourished. We’ll reassess in a couple of weeks with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count has dropped to 3.2, and hemoglobin is now 8.5. We’re watching for any signs of infection, but you’re not running a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? My energy is really low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The low counts may be related to chronic illness and malnutrition. Since you’re not bleeding or infected, we’ll support you with TPN and monitor. We won’t transfuse unless necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust you. The TPN seems to be helping—I feel a bit stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pneumonia is improving. The cough is gone, and your latest X-ray shows the opacity is resolving. We’re on day five of antibiotics—just one more day to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I can breathe better. Do I still have to stay NPO?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We tried food before and it triggered pain. For now, TPN is the safest way to nourish you. We’ll keep you on sips and meds only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. Your abdominal tenderness has improved. We’re planning for discharge in the next two days if things stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I’ll go home on TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A nurse will visit you at home to help with the TPN. You’ll continue it for at least two weeks, then see your GI doctor to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no food at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only sips of water and your medications. Even small meals could trigger another flare. It’s hard, but it’s the best way to let your pancreas heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your pneumonia is resolved, pain is much better, and you’re tolerating TPN well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about managing TPN at home. What if something goes wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse who’ll check the line, change dressings, and teach you what to watch for—like redness, fever, or pain at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue all your usual medications—bupropion, sertraline, oxybutynin, pantoprazole, and the fentanyl patch. We’ve also added ranitidine and a mouth rinse for reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hydromorphone and acetaminophen for breakthrough pain, and ondansetron for nausea. Use them as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll need weekly blood tests—basic metabolic panel, liver tests, and triglycerides—for the next few weeks. The results will go straight to your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially ready to go home. Your vitals are stable, lungs are clear, and belly is only mildly tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: TPN as scheduled, sips and meds only, no food. Follow up with your PCP and GI doctor. Call us if you develop fever, chills, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the visiting nurse will come tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll be there in the afternoon. You’ve done really well. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with idiopathic chronic pancreatitis was admitted with severe epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back and nausea, consistent with an acute flare. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, analgesia, and antiemetics. Her course was complicated by aspiration pneumonia, diagnosed on chest X-ray, and treated with a six-day course of levofloxacin and metronidazole. Due to persistent pain with oral intake, TPN was initiated via a left basilic vein PICC line placed on hospital day 6. Her symptoms improved with TPN, and she was discharged home with ongoing TPN, strict NPO status aside from sips and medications, and plans for outpatient follow-up with GI and PCP. Weekly lab monitoring was arranged.
